title: Delhi High Court Makes Amitabh Bachchan's Personality Rights Injunction Final and Binds Unidentified Infringers
meta_description: Delhi High Court turns a 2022 interim order into a final decree protecting Amitabh Bachchan's name, voice and image, binding unnamed online infringers too.
case_name: Amitabh Bachchan v. Rajat Nagi & Ors.
citation: CS(COMM) 819/2022 (decree dated 5 November 2026); neutral citation not yet available in reported sources
body: The Delhi High Court has turned a four-year-old interim order into a final decree in actor Amitabh Bachchan's suit over the commercial use of his name, image, voice and other personal attributes. Justice Purushaindra Kumar Kaurav decreed the suit, Amitabh Bachchan v. Rajat Nagi & Ors., on 5 November 2026, converting the ex-parte ad-interim injunction originally granted on 25 November 2022 into a permanent one.

That 2022 suit was filed after the actor's name and image turned up in a fake lottery scheme built around the Kaun Banega Crorepati brand, along with unauthorised merchandise, mobile applications and websites trading on his persona. At that stage the court granted an ad-interim injunction in rem. Such an order binds the named defendants and also anyone else engaged in the same kind of misuse, even a person unidentified at the time the suit was filed. Reports of the final decree say the court has now carried that structure through to the permanent order, so the injunction continues to reach unnamed or future infringers, commonly described as John Doe defendants, who copy the same conduct against the same persona. An in rem order of this kind is common in personality rights suits before the Delhi High Court precisely because online infringement rarely comes from a single, fixed set of actors. New websites, apps and sellers appear faster than a plaintiff can identify and sue them individually, so courts have leaned toward relief that covers the conduct rather than only the named parties who happened to be caught first.

Some of the originally named defendants, including Rajat Nagi, reportedly reached a settlement with the actor during the proceedings, while others such as Manoj Publications, Tamatina and Mahesh Patel remained contested. The decree brings the suit to a close on terms that permanently restrain commercial exploitation of the actor's persona without his consent, covering his name, image, voice, signature, style of talking and other personal attributes capable of identifying him.

The underlying cause of action rests on the personality right and right of publicity that Indian courts have recognised as part of the right to privacy and the right against unauthorised commercial appropriation of a person's identity. These rights do not depend on a specific statute. Courts have developed them through suits for passing off, infringement of trademark rights attached to a celebrity's name or image, and the broader tort of misappropriation, read together with constitutional protection of personal autonomy.

A decree of this kind has practical value beyond the four corners of the original dispute. Because the order binds unidentified infringers acting in a similar manner, a rights holder does not need to file a fresh suit each time a new website, app or seller appears using the same persona without consent. Enforcement can instead proceed through contempt or execution proceedings against the new infringer, once identified, by relying on the existing decree.

The Delhi High Court has handled a steady stream of personality rights litigation in recent years, involving several well-known public figures, and has developed a reasonably consistent approach: grant interim protection quickly where the facts show clear misuse for commercial gain, then move to a final decree once the record is complete. This case follows that pattern, with the court relying on the earlier interim order as the foundation for the permanent relief rather than reopening disputed facts that were never seriously contested by the parties who did not settle.

For businesses and individuals operating in Delhi NCR, the decision is a reminder that using a celebrity's name, voice or image in advertising, merchandise, apps or social media content, even indirectly through a fan page, a lookalike endorsement or an AI-generated likeness, carries real legal exposure. A decree already on record against similar conduct can be invoked quickly, without the delay of a fresh full trial.

Procedurally, the final decree appears to have been reached without a lengthy trial, since commercial suits before the Delhi High Court's IP Division can move to judgment on admitted or undisputed facts once the contesting defendants have had a fair hearing and no triable factual dispute remains on the core question of unauthorised commercial use. Four years between the interim order and the final decree is not unusual for a suit with multiple defendants, some of whom settled only after extended negotiation, while claims against non-appearing or untraceable online infringers were carried forward to the final hearing. The outcome also illustrates a recurring limit of this kind of litigation: a decree, however broadly framed, still depends on someone being identified before it can be enforced against them. Platforms hosting counterfeit merchandise, scam apps or impersonating accounts are not automatically compelled to act merely because a decree exists somewhere on record, and a rights holder typically still has to approach the relevant intermediary, domain registrar or app store with the order and seek a takedown, or return to court for specific directions against a newly identified respondent. The value of an in rem decree lies in removing the need to restart the suit from the beginning each time, not in making enforcement automatic.
why_it_matters: The ruling confirms that Delhi courts will convert interim personality rights protection into permanent, broadly worded decrees that reach future and unidentified infringers, beyond the parties originally sued. For anyone running a business, app or social media page that touches a public figure's name, voice or image, this raises the practical risk that enforcement can follow swiftly, since the rights holder does not have to start litigation over from scratch each time a new infringer appears.
card_summary: Delhi High Court has made permanent its 2022 injunction protecting Amitabh Bachchan's name, voice and image, and the final decree also binds unidentified future infringers.
card_tip: A personality rights decree framed to cover unnamed infringers lets a rights holder move straight to enforcement against a new copycat, instead of filing a fresh suit each time.
verification_notes: Topic chosen because this ruling was actively reported across LiveLaw-linked and mainstream outlets on 6-7 November 2026 and fits the demand-led intellectual property category; Delhi angle is direct since the Delhi High Court itself decided it. Case name, suit number CS(COMM) 819/2022, judge, and 5 November 2026 decree date confirmed via two independent reports (Bar and Bench, LawChakra); Free Press Journal's 7 November report corroborates the outcome though it does not give the exact decree date. Sources differ on the spelling of one settling defendant (Nagi vs Negi); the suit caption Nagi is used here. No official neutral citation or judgment copy was located in this search, so none is asserted; this is noted as unconfirmed rather than invented.
